pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 9–11 — an ocean ecosystem is an interconnected SYSTEM where living things (producers, consumers, decomposers) and non-living factors (temperature, salinity, light, currents) interact, and a change to one part cascades through the whole.
• Standards — UK (DfE Upper KS2): Y5 'describe the differences in the life cycles' and Y4/Y6 habitats and interdependence strands; builds on Y4 food chains toward systems thinking.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 5-LS2-1 (matter cycling among producers, consumers, decomposers and environment) and 3-LS4-4 / MS-LS2-4 (effects of changing the environment/physical factors) — living + non-living interaction is the anchor.
• Operational details: the leap from food WEB to ECOSYSTEM is adding the NON-LIVING (abiotic) factors — temperature, salinity, light, currents — and the roles decomposers play, then reasoning about how a change in one abiotic factor RIPPLES through the biotic community. Core move: perturb one variable (e.g. warmer water) and trace multi-step consequences. Emphasise systems thinking: parts are coupled, effects are indirect and sometimes surprising.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~9): names living and non-living parts and says they interact; Tier B (~10): names key abiotic factors and gives one living–nonliving link; Tier C (~11): traces how a change in one factor (temperature/light) cascades through the ecosystem via multiple steps.
bestPractices: Explicitly add the NON-LIVING factors to the food-web picture the child already has — temperature, salinity, light, currents — and show each shaping which organisms thrive.
Teach with perturbation: change ONE factor and have students trace the chain of consequences (warmer water → less plankton → fewer fish → hungry predators), reinforcing coupling.
Include decomposers and nutrient recycling so the system is a cycle, not just a one-way chain.
Use a concrete, coherent ecosystem (a kelp forest or reef) rather than a generic abstraction so interactions are specific and traceable.
Foreground indirect/surprising effects to build genuine systems thinking (a change far away, via currents, alters a local community).
keyRepresentations: A systems diagram linking biotic (producers/consumers/decomposers) and abiotic (temperature/salinity/light/currents) nodes
A perturbation panel: change one factor, watch multi-step ripples
A nutrient-cycling loop showing decomposers returning matter
A specific ecosystem map (kelp forest/reef) with its living and non-living parts labelled
commonMisconceptions: Thinking an ecosystem is just the animals/plants (biotic) and forgetting the non-living factors that shape it.
Believing effects are local and direct — not anticipating indirect, multi-step, or distant ripples.
Confusing a food web (energy among organisms) with an ecosystem (organisms + physical environment as one system).
Ignoring decomposers/recycling, treating the system as a one-way flow rather than a cycle.
Assuming ecosystems are static/balanced forever rather than dynamic systems that respond to change.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11: an ocean ecosystem is an interconnected system where living parts (producers, consumers, decomposers) and non-living factors (temperature, salinity, light, currents) interact, so a change to one part ripples through the whole. The core learning move is perturbation: change ONE factor and trace the multi-step, sometimes indirect consequences. Activities build from naming living/non-living parts (Tier A), to linking a non-living factor to the living community (Tier B), to tracing a cascade through several steps (Tier C). A manipulable ecosystem model is the centrepiece, supported by a labelled systems diagram, targeted checks, and what-if dialogue.

activities.title: Run the kelp forest: perturb one factor, trace the ripple
feedback: If a learner says only heat-sensitive animals are affected: follow one link at a time from the warmed water to a producer, then to its consumers, making the knock-on connections visible.
If a learner predicts a one-step effect only: ask them to keep going — 'and then what happens to the animals that ate that one?' — until they reach something two or more steps away.
Reinforce when a learner spontaneously names an indirect or distant effect: this is the systems-thinking goal.
Note that warming need not always thin plankton — depending on conditions it could make plankton bloom or crash — so the exact chain is one example of coupling, not a fixed rule.

If a learner expects the system to snap back automatically, discuss thresholds: small changes may be absorbed, but a big or sustained one can flip the system to a new state (kelp forest becoming an urchin barren).
activities.rationale: The defining idea — coupled living/non-living parts where changing one ripples through the rest — is a dynamic system behaviour that a manipulable model lets a learner drive and observe. Perturbing a single factor and tracing consequences directly targets the Tier C cascade-reasoning goal. Standards frame modelling matter movement among producers, consumers, decomposers and the environment, and reasoning about how changes to physical factors disrupt a system.
sourceClaims: NGSS 5-LS2-1 asks students to model matter movement among producers, consumers, decomposers and the environment; MS-LS2-4 addresses how changes to physical/biological components disrupt an ecosystem.
Ocean ecosystems are shaped by abiotic factors — temperature, salinity, light and currents — interacting with living communities, and changes to these physical factors propagate through the system.
learnerActions: Explore a kelp-forest model with adjustable factors for water temperature, light, salinity and current, and a community of producers (phytoplankton, the plant-like plankton, and kelp), consumers (zooplankton, urchins, fish, sea otters) and decomposers.
Change ONE factor only — e.g. nudge the water warmer — and watch over time how the community responds step by step.
Before each change, predict out loud which living thing will be hit first and what will follow two or three steps along the chain.

After watching, trace the actual chain in order (for example: warmer water → plankton thin out → the plankton-feeders that ate them dwindle → their predators go hungry → decomposer workload shifts) and compare it with your prediction. Treat this as one plausible outcome, not the only one.
Run several different perturbations (e.g. cloudier water so less light gets through) and note any effect that surprised you or reached a creature you would not have connected to that factor.
State in your own words why touching just one non-living factor moved the whole web.
activities.intendedInsight: An ocean ecosystem is living AND non-living parts locked together; changing one factor cascades through multiple steps, and effects can be indirect and surprising rather than staying contained to one species.

activities.title: Map the system: living and non-living parts linked
feedback: If a learner lists only animals and plants, prompt: 'Where do temperature, light, salinity and currents go on this map?' to show they belong inside the system.
If a learner draws only one-way arrows, ask what happens to dead matter and nutrients, guiding them to close the loop through decomposers.
activities.rationale: A labelled, explorable diagram lays out the vocabulary and structure clearly, giving the parts and links that the cascade reasoning builds on. It presents structure well but is static on its own, so it scaffolds rather than replaces running a perturbation.
learnerActions: Study a labelled ecosystem web showing producers, consumers, decomposers and the non-living factors (temperature, salinity, light, currents).
Select a non-living factor (e.g. temperature or light) and identify which organisms it affects and how.
Sketch or describe at least one first-order effect: 'if this rose, then ...'.
Add the decomposers and show how they return matter to the system, making it a cycle rather than a one-way chain.
activities.intendedInsight: An ecosystem's parts — living and non-living — are connected into a structure, and non-living factors are members of the system, not just a backdrop.

activities.title: Check your understanding: parts, definitions and cascades
feedback: For sorting: if temperature or light is placed outside the ecosystem, clarify that these are parts of the system, not just its setting. A sort checks classification but does not itself require the learner to trace a cascade, so pair it with the scenario step.
For the scenario: if the answer is 'only the heat-sensitive animals change', ask for the next link in the chain and the one after that.

Model answer for the warming scenario: probably not — because the parts are connected, a season of water a few degrees warmer can weaken the kelp (a producer) or make plankton bloom or crash; that can change food for the animals that eat them, which can change their predators and which species survive there, so the effect is likely to spread rather than stay contained, even though the exact chain depends on conditions.
activities.rationale: Targeted questions check all three evidence goals — naming abiotic factors, distinguishing web from ecosystem, and tracing a cascade — which are the standards-derived evidence for this topic. As a companion check it verifies recall and scenario reasoning; on its own, selection and recall do not elicit independent construction of a cascade, so it follows the model work.
sourceClaims: NGSS 5-LS2-1 asks students to model matter movement among producers, consumers, decomposers and the environment; MS-LS2-4 addresses how changes to physical/biological components disrupt an ecosystem.
learnerActions: Sort items into living and non-living parts of the ecosystem.
Name the key non-living factors that affect ocean life: temperature, salinity, light, currents.
Distinguish a food web (energy among organisms) from an ecosystem (organisms plus their physical environment as one system).
Given a scenario — e.g. the water warms a few degrees for a whole season — trace the multi-step ripple and explain whether the effect stays contained.
activities.intendedInsight: Confirms the learner can name the system's parts, tell a food web from an ecosystem, and follow a change through several steps rather than only naming isolated parts.

activities.title: What-if with a marine ecologist: predict the chain
feedback: If the learner names only isolated parts, prompt them to connect two of them with a 'because' or 'so then' to build a chain.
Push on thresholds: ask whether the system always returns to normal, or whether a large or sustained change could leave it permanently different.
activities.rationale: Verbal what-if questioning probes systems reasoning and can be used during teaching to prompt prediction and explanation. It supplements driving a live model, where coupled multi-step ripples are easier to see; the two are complementary rather than ranked.
learnerActions: Respond to a marine ecologist (real or role-played) posing 'what happens if the water warms?' or 'what if less light gets through?'
Predict the chain of consequences aloud, step by step, before any answer is revealed.

Answer probing follow-ups: name one living thing hit first, then follow the chain to something two steps away; identify which non-living parts could change the animals; judge whether a small change could tip the whole system into something different.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating a cascade in conversation surfaces whether the learner can follow a connected chain or only name isolated parts.

constraints: The systems diagram presents structure and vocabulary but does not itself run a perturbation cascade; use it as a scaffold before or alongside the model, not as the whole lesson.

The check-your-understanding questions assess naming and scenario reasoning; recognition/selection does not elicit the independent construction of a cascade, so pair them with the model and/or the learner tracing a chain themselves.
Use a concrete, coherent ecosystem (a kelp forest or reef) rather than a generic abstraction so interactions are specific and traceable.
Include decomposers and nutrient recycling so the system reads as a cycle, not a one-way chain.
Treat ecosystems as dynamic: small changes may be absorbed, but large or sustained ones can flip the system to a new state; avoid implying nature always rebalances automatically.
A spatial/3D version could add immersion; the coupling and cascade reasoning can be conveyed with a 2D model whose controls and cause-traces are visible, so 3D is an option, not a requirement.
Present the warming → plankton chain as one plausible outcome (plankton may thin, bloom or crash depending on conditions), not as a fixed law.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; both sources were marked verified:false in the row and have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original entry asserted the manipulable model is the one artefact that makes the systems behaviour 'felt' and that 3D 'adds nothing'/does not deepen the insight; these comparative-necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been softened to scoped proposals with stated affordances and limits.

The NOAA abiotic-propagation claim is attached to the model activity as content-validity support for its cascade-tracing move; it is not evidence that a manipulable model is more effective than other media.

The warming example lists both 'plankton bloom' and 'plankton crash' as possible outcomes; this is realistic (direction depends on conditions) but means the specific chain used in the model/feedback is one plausible scenario, not the only outcome.

Threshold/tipping-point content (kelp forest to urchin barren) is pedagogically reasonable but depends on severity and duration of the disturbance; keep it as conditional discussion rather than a guaranteed result.
In a kelp forest, urchins are typically kelp grazers rather than plankton feeders; the chain wording has been kept generic ('plankton-feeders that ate them') to avoid implying urchins graze plankton.

probeDeeper: You changed the temperature — name one LIVING thing it hits first, then follow the chain to something two steps away.
Which parts of this ecosystem are non-living, and could changing one of THEM change the animals?
What if instead the water got cloudier so less light got through — would that stay contained, or spread? How?
Is there any point where a small change could tip the whole system into something completely different?
assess.correctAnswer: No — an ecosystem is a system where living things and non-living factors (temperature, salinity, light, currents) all interact, so a change in one factor ripples through the whole thing. Warmer water can weaken the kelp (a producer), or make plankton bloom or crash; that changes food for the animals that eat them, which changes their predators, and it can also change which species can survive there at all. Because the parts are connected, a change to one non-living factor cascades — it doesn't stay contained to a single species.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'A change affects only the one thing it touches' — treats the ecosystem as separate creatures, not a connected system.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the web on the board and follow one arrow at a time from the warmed water to a producer to its consumers; make the connections visible.
errorPatterns.distractor: Only the animals that dislike warm water are affected — the rest of the ecosystem carries on unchanged.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says warming only bothers the heat-sensitive animals; can't trace a knock-on effect to anything else.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'An ecosystem is just the animals (and maybe plants)' — leaves out the non-living factors entirely.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort a set of cards into living and non-living 'parts of the system'; show that light and temperature are members of the ecosystem, not just its backdrop.
errorPatterns.distractor: Temperature isn't part of the ecosystem — only the plants and animals are.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Lists only living things when asked what's in the ecosystem; doesn't mention temperature, light, salinity or currents.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Nature always balances itself back' — assumes any disturbance is automatically corrected with no lasting change.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss thresholds: small changes may be absorbed, but a big or sustained one can flip the system to a new state (kelp forest to urchin barren).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 'it'll just go back to normal'; treats resilience as guaranteed rather than limited.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks a change affects only the directly-touched species, or omits non-living factors from the ecosystem.
responseLevels.full: Traces a change in one factor through the system step by step (factor → producer → consumer → predator), explains that interaction is what makes it a system, and transfers the reasoning to a new disturbance such as reduced light.
responseLevels.partial: Names living and non-living parts (temperature, light, salinity, currents, producers, consumers) but lists them — can't trace how a change in one cascades through the others.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In a kelp-forest ecosystem the water warms up by a few degrees for a whole season. A child says 'the only thing that changes is the animals that don't like warm water — everything else stays the same'. Do you think a change to just the temperature would stay contained like that? Talk me through what happens, and why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks of the ecosystem as a list of independent creatures says the change affects only the temperature-sensitive animals; a child with a systems view traces a chain from the non-living factor through producers to consumers and predators. Asking them to 'talk through what happens' exposes whether they can follow a cascade or only name isolated parts.
